cards.explanation: The answer is slave. The writer says, "The princess of the provinces has become a slave." Look at the drop in that one line, friends. Princess to slave is a long way down, and the writer just says it plainly.

The answer is her enemies. The writer says, "All her friends have betrayed her; they have become her enemies." That's a different kind of hurt than a stranger turning on you. These were the ones she counted on.

The answer is False, and the text is blunt about it. "Among all her lovers there is no one to comfort her." She weeps aloud in the night, with tears upon her cheeks. The verse adds that all her friends have betrayed her and become her enemies, so nobody is coming. (Lamentations 1:2)

The answer is no place to rest. The writer says Judah "…dwells among the nations but finds no place to rest." She's living somewhere, but she can't settle. I know that feeling of being somewhere without being home, friends.

The answer is her many transgressions. The writer says, "For the LORD has brought her grief because of her many transgressions." The text gives the reason right there, so we don't have to guess. This is the poem being honest about the cause, and that honesty comes back later in the poem.

The answer is that they're too weak to flee. The writer says her princes "…lack the strength to flee in the face of the hunter." Deer with no pasture have nothing left in the tank, friends. They can't even run.
The answer is False. The writer says, "Her enemies looked upon her, laughing at her downfall." They didn't look away, they looked and laughed. That's a heavy line, and the poem doesn't soften it.

The answer is False. The writer says, "she did not consider her end," and calls her downfall "astounding." Nothing in the verse says she saw it coming from a long way off. And the verse says there was "…no one to comfort her."

The answer is the LORD. The poem cries, "Look, O LORD, on my affliction, for the enemy has triumphed!" When nobody else is there to comfort her, the cry goes up to Him. I think that's a strong thing to do in the middle of all this, friends.

The answer is forbidden. The poem says she has seen the nations enter her sanctuary, "…those You had forbidden to enter Your assembly." God had forbidden it, and she saw them enter her sanctuary. That's the heartbreak in this line.

The answer is True. The text says, "They have traded their treasures for food to keep themselves alive." Verse 11 also says all her people "…groan as they search for bread." Treasures traded for food, just to stay alive.

The answer is if any sorrow compares. The poem asks, "Is there any sorrow like mine, which was inflicted on me, which the LORD made me suffer on the day of His fierce anger?" It's a cry to everyone passing by to stop and look. I think it's the sound of someone who needs to be seen, friends.

The answer is True. The poem asks about the sorrow "…which the LORD made me suffer on the day of His fierce anger?" The poem says it plainly and doesn't dodge. It's a heavy line, so we'll let it sit for a moment.
The answer is False. The poem says, "He spread a net for my feet and turned me back." This net catches feet and turns the speaker around. It's a picture of being stopped, not carried.
The answer is neck. The poem says the transgressions "…are draped over my neck…" That's what a yoke does, friends. It sits on the neck and makes every step heavier.

The answer is False. The poem says, "The Lord has rejected all the mighty men in my midst…" It goes on to say He "…has summoned an army against me to crush my young warriors." The mighty men aren't being honored.

The answer is that his neighbors become his foes. The poem says, "The LORD has decreed against Jacob that his neighbors become his foes." Jacob here means his people. The people living right next door turned into enemies.

The answer is righteous. The poem says, "The LORD is righteous, yet I rebelled against His command." Look at what the speaker does here, friends. The speaker doesn't blame anyone else and says the LORD is righteous.

The answer is the young men and maidens. The poem says, "My young men and maidens have gone into captivity." These are the young ones, and the poem asks everyone to look at that suffering. I think it's one of the hardest lines in the chapter.
The answer is the speaker's distress. The poem says, "See, O LORD, how distressed I am!" The speaker doesn't dress it up and just asks to be seen. I think that's honest prayer, friends.
The answer is True. The poem says of the enemies, "they are glad that You have caused it." They heard about the trouble and they're glad. That's a lonely thing to read, even in a poem.

The answer is to end up the same way. The poem asks the LORD to bring the day He has announced "…so that they may become like me." Then verse 22 asks Him to "…deal with them as You have dealt with me…" That's the speaker's plea, and the poem doesn't hide how raw it is.
